extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions' Title IX administrators, investigators, decisionmakers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements and permissible options for conducting live questioning in Title IX sex-based harassment grievance procedures at postsecondary institutions, including individual meetings, live hearings, question proposal processes, evidence access, and limits on questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-questioning process enabling credibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must include a live-questioning process that enables the decisionmaker to assess credibility of parties and witnesses to the extent credibility is both in dispute and relevant to one or more allegations of sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to provide basic principles of fairness and due process while allowing recipients flexibility in implementation. The live-questioning process should be designed to produce reliable outcomes and account for the risk of erroneous deprivation and the potential for re-traumatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible forms of live questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Live questioning, including questions and follow-up questions proposed by the parties, may occur in individual meetings with the investigator or decisionmaker, or in a live hearing with questions asked by the decisionmaker or the party's advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may choose which permissible form to use; they are not required to conduct live, adversarial hearings in all cases and may eschew live hearings if appropriate under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-proposed questions and who asks them
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party may propose questions that the party wants asked of any party or witness; those proposed questions must be asked either by the investigator or decisionmaker during individual meetings (if no live hearing) or (in a live hearing) by the decisionmaker or by the party's advisor, depending on the institution's chosen process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a postsecondary institution chooses not to use advisor-conducted questioning, it must allow parties to propose questions to be asked by the investigator or decisionmaker. Proposed questions must satisfy relevance and permissibility criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording or transcript requirement when no live hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a postsecondary institution chooses not to hold a live hearing, it must provide each party with an audio or audiovisual recording or transcript of the individual meetings with enough time for the party to have a reasonable opportunity to propose follow-up questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement (new §106.46(f)(1)(i)(C)) helps replicate some aspects of live questioning by permitting parties to review statements and propose follow-ups; the Department acknowledges this is not identical to live cross-examination but establishes a baseline procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information gathered in individual meetings is part of the evidentiary record
rubrics_metrics.description: Information gathered at individual meetings with parties and witnesses is part of the evidence or investigative report and must be included in the materials covered by §106.46(e)(6)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must provide equal opportunity to access either the relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence or the same written investigative report that accurately summarizes this evidence, and provide a reasonable opportunity to review and respond prior to the determination whether sex-based harassment occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on permissible questions (relevance and impermissible evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions proposed by the parties must be relevant and not otherwise impermissible under §§106.2 and 106.45(b)(7), and may not be unclear or harassing under §106.46(f)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department specifically notes limits such as §106.45(b)(7)(iii) on evidence that relates to a complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct; institutions may decline to ask questions that are duplicative, harassing, or otherwise impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and frequency of individual meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be one or more individual meetings, including follow-up meetings with parties and witnesses, as needed to establish facts, assess credibility, and ask follow-up questions; the appropriate number will vary depending on facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions are not expected to hold an endless cycle of meetings; if follow-up questions are duplicative or designed to harass rather than elicit relevant information, the institution may decline additional meetings. §§106.2, 106.45(b)(7), and 106.46(f) together prevent an overly long or burdensome process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may conduct individual meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual meetings may be conducted by the investigator, decisionmaker, or both, at the institution's discretion; whether a panel must be fully present is left to the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of who attends, the institution must ensure the process enables a decisionmaker to adequately assess credibility and that the decisionmaker determines whether proposed questions are relevant and permissible before they are posed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual meeting option
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations precludes a recipient from conducting individual meetings virtually using technology that enables the decisionmaker or investigator and the party or witness to simultaneously see and hear one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions have discretion to hold individual meetings virtually or in person, subject to other procedural requirements and accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for who asks questions at live hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a postsecondary institution chooses to conduct a live hearing under §106.46(g), the process must allow the decisionmaker to ask relevant and permissible questions, and either: (a) allow each party to propose questions to be asked by the decisionmaker, or (b) allow each party's advisor to ask such questions, so long as they are not unclear or harassing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department did not intend to require advisor-conducted questioning in live hearings; institutions may choose between advisor questioning or decisionmaker-posed party-proposed questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker filtering of proposed questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a question is posed, the decisionmaker must determine whether a question proposed by the parties is relevant and not otherwise impermissible under §§106.2 and 106.45(b)(7) or unclear or harassing under §106.46(f)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gatekeeping role is essential to prevent harassment, irrelevant inquiry, or the admission of impermissible evidence, and to ensure questioning is focused on assessing credibility and eliciting relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline procedures vs. additional procedural protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations establish baseline procedures that recipients must follow; any recipient that concludes its constitutional obligations, other sources of authority, or other circumstances require additional procedural protections may provide such protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions remain free to maintain more protective procedures (for example, the 2020 amendments' live-hearing model) if they deem those necessary under law or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Mathews balancing and trauma risk
rubrics_metrics.description: In designing live-questioning procedures, the Department balanced the Mathews factors (risk of erroneous deprivation and benefit of additional procedures, and the government's interest including burden and cost) and considered the potential for re-traumatization of complainants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final approach aims to reduce the likelihood of re-traumatization while allowing for credibility testing and reliable outcomes; institutions should likewise tailor procedures mindful of these considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt, equitable, and meaningful opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must be prompt and equitable and provide the parties, including the respondent, with a meaningful opportunity to be heard and respond, and be designed to produce reliable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should protect the interests of all parties while accounting for administrative and financial burden on institutions and the need to allocate resources to education and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method within a particular complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution is not required to use the same method of assessing credibility for all live hearings, but it must use the same method for assessing credibility for each party or witness within resolution of a particular complaint (absent disability or language-access accommodations or auxiliary aids/services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must articulate consistent principles in their written grievance procedures for how they will determine which method of assessing credibility will apply (for example, when advisor questioning will be used), so the educational community knows in advance what method will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation of state/federal case law or other legal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in §106.46(f)(1) precludes a postsecondary institution from choosing to use a live hearing with questioning by an advisor if required under applicable Federal or State case law or other legal obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulation provides flexibility, but institutions must comply with any other binding legal requirements that mandate specific procedures.
